summary: Phishing-triggered OAuth approval redirects causing suspicious consent events across multiple internal accounts
description:
Issue summary:
A number of engineers reported receiving spear-phishing emails that contained a call-to-action link labelled 'Approve new login'. When several recipients clicked the link from corp email, our SSO (Okta) logs show OAuth 'consent' or 'grant' events originating from the redirecting domain instead of our normal app flow. The events resulted in issuance of short-lived tokens tied to legitimate accounts.

Impact:
- 7 internal accounts (engineering and infra) observed suspicious consent/grant events between 2026-03-10T02:15Z and 2026-03-10T03:05Z.
- No confirmed data exfiltration as of last update; tokens were short-lived and used in limited API requests.
- Potential for lateral movement if tokens were used to authorize additional integrations.

Timeline (as reported):
- 2026-03-10 02:12 UTC: First user reports emailed to #security.
- 2026-03-10 02:20 UTC: SSO team triaged anomalous OAuth grants for app-client-id 'redwood-consent-proxy'.
- 2026-03-10 02:35 UTC: SRE observed ephemeral API calls from IP ranges associated with third-party cloud provider; calls were limited and rate-low.
- 2026-03-10 02:50 UTC: Initial mitigation: block domain and suspend affected sessions.

Steps to reproduce (observed pattern):
1) User receives email from external domain spoofing vendor invoice notifications.
2) Stimulus link redirects through a shortener and then to a page that initiates an OAuth flow pointing at our Okta authorization endpoint with a forged redirect_uri.
3) Browser shows a small consent/approval modal mimicking an MFA/approval UX asking user to 'Approve'.
4) If user clicks, Okta logs a grant/consent event for a third-party client id, followed by token issuance and a redirect to the attacker-controlled URL.

Observed behavior & logs (examples):
- Okta event IDs: 0oa1a2b3c4d5e6f7g8 (user: j.kim), 0oa9z8y7x6w5v4u3t2 (user: l.barnes).
- Token usage: Short lived (<=10m) access tokens used to call our internal metrics ingestion endpoint once per token.
- Reverse DNS and WHOIS for redirect domain show recent registration and DNS proxied via CDN.

Hypothesis:
This is a targeted phishing campaign leveraging an OAuth redirect trick to obtain delegated tokens via user consent rather than credential theft. Attack likely opportunistic for accounts with elevated access to internal APIs.

Immediate mitigations applied:
- Blocked the malicious domains at email gateway and network proxy.
- Revoked all active OAuth grants associated with the suspicious client-id via Okta admin API.
- Forced re-auth for 7 affected users and rotated API keys for any services they could access.
- Added a temporary app-level policy to require explicit admin approval for new OAuth app-consents from unverified clients.

Open questions / next steps:
- Confirm full scope: search Okta and audit logs for similar grants in last 7 days (task assigned to SSO).
- Forensic review of API calls made with the tokens to identify any attempted data pulls.
- Assess whether the attacker registered a malicious app in any partner/SaaS connectors.
- Evaluate adding additional consent UI hardening and user training to reduce click-throughs.

Owner (triage): Marco Reyes (SSO / INFRA)

Attachments / evidence links:
- Slack thread: #security (https://slack.redwood.internal/archives/C02ABCDEFG)
- Okta admin export (s3://sec-logs/okta/2026-03-10-grants.csv)
- Packet captures: s3://sec-logs/pcap/oauth-redirect-2026-03-10.pcap
investigation_notes:
Initial investigation indicates no service account password compromise. Tokens were used for low-volume API calls likely to test validity. IPs trace to cloud provider egress addresses; enrichment suggests use of residential-like proxies. We pulled telemetry from API gateway and have quarantined the few target endpoints for deeper analysis. SSO team will perform a full grant history sweep and export all 'consent' events for the last 72 hours.

Hypotheses tested so far:
- Compromised session cookie: unlikely, session timestamps show issuance concurrent with consent events.
- Credential stuffing: unlikely, no failed auth spikes.
- Malicious OAuth client registered in third-party app store: possible, investigating vendor/partner connectors.

Preliminary conclusion: attacker relied on user consent via phishing redirect. Remedy requires both technical controls and user education.
comments: 2026-03-10 02:25 UTC - Samir Gupta (SRE): Observed 3 token uses from 18.204.12.9 hitting /internal-metrics but traffic pattern low. Suspect probe. Added IP to block list.

2026-03-10 02:32 UTC - Priya Nair (Security): Temporarily suspended all active sessions for affected users and initiated Okta grant revocation. Notifying Legal if evidence of data access beyond probes is found.

2026-03-10 03:10 UTC - Marco Reyes (SSO): Revoke completed for client-id 'redwood-consent-proxy'. Added app policy requiring admin approval for unverified apps. Will deliver sweep results by 2026-03-12.
2026-03-11 09:05 UTC - Aisha Patel (Reporter): Confirmed affected users have completed re-auth, no further suspicious emails reported in the last 24h. User outreach drafted and sent.
2026-03-12 14:20 UTC - Forensics (sec-forensics): Found one API call that requested a list of service names; no exfiltration detected. Continuing log correlation for lateral activity.
resolution: Mitigations in place: domains blocked, OAuth grants revoked, sessions forced re-auth, API keys rotated where applicable. Admin-approval policy for new OAuth apps deployed. Forensics did not find confirmed data exfiltration. Case remains open pending full grant sweep and final post-incident review.
follow_up_actions: Complete Okta grant sweep across 30-day window
Finalize post-incident report and playbook update
Roll out targeted user training on 'OAuth approval' phishing patterns
Consider implementing automated detection for unusual consent-origin domains
